articles.title: The American World Cup Introduced Ad Breaks—and Everyone Absolutely Hates It
America Is Already Losing the World Cup for Hotel Bookings

vocab.articleQuote: …there's been just one problem with shoehorning [soccer] into the American way of televised sports.
vocab.inContext: It means forcing soccer — a sport built on nonstop play — into a TV format designed for sports that have lots of natural stoppages, even though it doesn't fit comfortably.
vocab.meaning: To shoehorn something is to force it into a space, schedule, or role that's really too small or the wrong shape for it.
examples: The teacher tried to shoehorn three lab experiments into a single 45-minute class, so we rushed through all of them.
He shoehorned a quote from his favorite movie into his history essay, even though it didn't really belong.

vocab.articleQuote: Fox Sports…didn't capitalize on that value simply by dropping in a brief ad for each pause in the action.
vocab.inContext: Fox didn't just take advantage of the valuable ad time in the obvious, minimal way — it packed in far more commercials than one ad per break.
vocab.meaning: To capitalize on something is to make the most of an opportunity or advantage. (It's related to 'capital'/money, but in this sense it's about seizing a chance, not just cash.)
examples: After the goalie slipped, our striker capitalized on the open net and scored.
She capitalized on the long weekend to finish the project she'd been putting off.

vocab.articleQuote: Visa concerns and the U.S. political climate that many foreigners perceive as unwelcoming also dissuaded some…from traveling to the U.S.
vocab.inContext: Worries about visas and an unfriendly mood convinced some international fans not to make the trip.
vocab.meaning: To dissuade someone is to persuade them not to do something — the opposite of 'persuade,' which talks someone into it.
examples: My parents tried to dissuade me from staying up all night before the exam.
Bad reviews dissuaded us from seeing the movie this weekend.

vocab.articleQuote: …the foreign host cities hold a number of advantages…including often more rabid soccer fans and overall affordability.
vocab.inContext: It describes fans whose enthusiasm for soccer is extreme and intense — the kind who pack stadiums and travel for matches.
vocab.meaning: Rabid means extreme, fanatical, or out of control in your enthusiasm or opinions. (It literally describes an animal with rabies, which is where the 'uncontrolled' sense comes from.)
examples: He's a rabid fan of the series — he reread every book the week before the finale came out.
The argument turned rabid, with neither side willing to listen to the other.

concepts.name: Broadcast rights
concepts.articleQuote: Fox Sports, which holds the English-language rights to the tournament in the U.S.…
concepts.inContext: Fox paid for the exclusive right to show the World Cup in English in the United States, which is why American viewers watch it on Fox rather than wherever they like.
concepts.meaning: Broadcast rights are the exclusive permission a network or streaming service buys to show an event — a game, a concert, a show. Whoever owns the rights controls where you can watch it and charges advertisers or subscribers to earn their money back. It's why one big game might be available on only a single channel or app.

concepts.name: The attention economy
concepts.articleQuote: …a 30-second spot during early games costs some brands roughly $200,000, but jumps to around $750,000 when the U.S. national team is playing.
concepts.inContext: A commercial slot costs far more during the U.S. game because far more people are watching — advertisers are really paying for all those eyeballs.
concepts.meaning: In 'free' or ad-supported media, the audience's attention is the product being sold. Advertisers pay the platform for access to your eyes and time, and the price rises with the size and value of the audience. That's why the most-watched moments cost advertisers the most — and why so much of what you watch is designed to keep you watching.

concepts.name: Dynamic pricing (supply and demand)
concepts.articleQuote: Host Hotels & Resorts…is already seeing a 38% jump in average daily rates from transient travelers for the tournament period.
concepts.inContext: Hotels raised their nightly rates sharply for the World Cup because they expected lots of visitors competing for a limited number of rooms.
concepts.meaning: Dynamic pricing means prices move with demand instead of staying fixed. When many buyers want a limited supply, sellers raise prices (a $20,000 resale ticket, a surged hotel room); when demand is weak, prices fall to attract buyers. It's the everyday engine behind airfares, concert tickets, and ride-share surge pricing.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost
concepts.articleQuote: Occupancy is flat…because the World Cup has so far largely displaced other business he typically counts on during the summer weeks.
concepts.inContext: Even with the World Cup in town, the hotel isn't fuller than usual — the soccer visitors mostly replaced the regular summer guests it would have had anyway, so it didn't really gain.
concepts.meaning: The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next-best thing you give up to make it. World Cup guests aren't pure profit if they crowd out customers a hotel would have had regardless. Counting only what you gain — and ignoring what you gave up — makes a deal look better than it really is. (Same logic with your Saturday: its true cost includes whatever else you could have done.)

quiz.question: A 30-second commercial during early World Cup games cost some brands about $200,000, but the price jumped to roughly $750,000 when the U.S. national team played. What best explains the increase?
options: Ads during U.S. games were required to be twice as long.
Many more people watch the U.S. team, so that audience is worth more to advertisers.
Fox Sports accidentally underpriced the early games.
FIFA charges teams a fee to appear in commercials.
quiz.explanation: In an ad-supported broadcast, advertisers pay for attention — the bigger the audience, the more a slot is worth.

quiz.question: Resale tickets to the World Cup final were selling for more than $20,000 a seat. This price is best explained by —
options: broadcast rights
a hydration break
limited seats meeting very strong demand, which pushes prices up
the cost of building the stadium
quiz.explanation: Dynamic pricing: when a scarce, highly wanted item meets strong demand, the price rises.

quiz.question: One hotel executive said the World Cup left his occupancy 'flat' because the soccer visitors largely 'displaced' the regular summer guests he normally gets. Why does that matter?
options: It proves the World Cup doubled his profits.
The event isn't a real gain if it just replaces customers he would have had anyway.
It means the hotel had to close during the games.
It shows that hotel rooms are free during big events.
quiz.explanation: That's opportunity cost — the true benefit counts what you gave up, not just what you took in.

quiz.question: The article describes the 'problem with shoehorning' soccer into American-style TV. To shoehorn something means to —
options: advertise it widely
force it into a space or format it doesn't really fit
make it far more popular
cancel it at the last minute
quiz.explanation: To shoehorn is to cram something into a space, schedule, or role that's too small or the wrong shape for it.

quiz.question: Visa worries and an unwelcoming climate 'dissuaded' some fans from traveling to the U.S. To dissuade someone is to —
options: persuade them not to do something
strongly encourage them to do something
charge them extra money
help them plan a trip
quiz.explanation: Dissuade is the opposite of persuade — it means to talk or push someone out of doing something.
